activities.description: Paul Sutter talks about the size of the Milky Way galaxy and how it was discovered.

narrativeProgression.description: Paul Sutter poses the question, "How big is the universe?"
He explains that the observable universe is about 90 billion light-years across, but the actual size of the entire universe is unknown.
He discusses the historical debate about the size of the universe, mentioning different observations that yielded conflicting results.
He introduces the "Great Debate" or the "Curtis-Shapley Debate," where two prominent astronomers argued about the size and nature of the universe.
He focuses on the role of spiral nebulae in this debate, highlighting the uncertainty surrounding their nature.
He asks whether these nebulae were part of our galaxy or something else entirely.
He reveals that the answer came in the early 1920s with Edwin Hubble's work.
He explains Henrietta Swan Leavitt's discovery of the relationship between the period and luminosity of Cepheid variable stars, which enabled astronomers to measure distances.
He describes how Hubble used Cepheid variables in the Andromeda Nebula to determine its immense distance, proving it was a separate galaxy.
He concludes that the Milky Way is an isolated clump of stars, gas, and dust, separated by vast distances from other galaxies.
He discusses the origin of the name "Milky Way," explaining its connection to the appearance of a band of light across the sky.
He mentions Galileo's observation of the Milky Way through a telescope, revealing it to be composed of countless individual stars.
He explains the flat, pancake-like shape of the Milky Way, indicating our position within the galaxy.
He describes the spiral arms of the Milky Way and our location on the Orion Arm.

He states that the Milky Way is an average spiral galaxy with a supermassive black hole at its center, a decent magnetic field, a reasonable star formation rate, and has existed in its present form for about 9 billion years.
He briefly mentions the future collision of the Milky Way with the Andromeda galaxy.
He emphasizes the centuries of observations required to develop our understanding of the Milky Way.
He reiterates the key revelation that spiral nebulae are actually galaxies in their own right.
He promises to discuss other types of galaxies and their formation in the next episode.

scenes.thematicElements: The vastness and scale of the universe. The evolution of our understanding of the Milky Way. The interconnectedness of astronomical discoveries.
scenes.title: Introduction and Evolution of Understanding the Milky Way

It’s time for school! The Astro101 series will cover some of the most important questions in astronomy. In today’s lesson, we’ll have: What is a galaxy? What does our own galaxy look like? What are the different kinds of galaxies, and how did they get that way? I discuss these questions and more in today’s Ask a Spaceman!

Follow all the show updates at http://www.askaspaceman.com, and help support the show at http://www.patreon.com/pmsutter

Keep those questions about space, science, astronomy, astrophysics, and cosmology coming to #AskASpaceman for COMPLETE KNOWLEDGE OF TIME AND SPACE! Music by Jason Grady and Nick Bain.
